voice_event.text:
Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pilate, truly crucified, and truly died. Ignatius wrote it that way - truly, again and again - because some among our neighbors were saying he only seemed to suffer. Ignatius wrote: “So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. He came from the family of David, and he was also Mary's son. He was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified, and he died. Beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth saw it happen. He was also truly raised from the dead, because his Father brought him back to life. In the same way, his Father will raise us too, who believe in him, through Christ Jesus. Without him, we do not have the true life.”

And he was truly raised, the same way the Father will raise us. When we gave thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our word for that thanksgiving - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, which he made known to us through Jesus. That is who he was to us: a real man, born and raised and put to death, the one through whom the Father's own life reached us.

glosses.plain_meaning: The thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks is given. The community returns to this table again and again, to be formed once more into one body.
glosses.quick_meaning: The thanksgiving - the bread-and-cup meal at the center of the community's life; its form varied from church to church.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Is that what we call transubstantiation?' - the later word answers a question this world had not yet asked in that form. What it held is strong enough in its own words: Ignatius calls the eucharist 'the flesh of our Saviour Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins' - against those who denied the body's reality - and the Didache's prayers give thanks for life and knowledge. Between those two registers no single doctrine of the elements is yet settled.
false_friend: a uniform ritual with fixed prayers (the form varies community to community)

Before that, he had already gone looking through other philosophies. He turned the old man's words over in his mind, and found this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. And if you are asking what Jesus did - he ate and drank, he was persecuted under Pilate, he was crucified and died, and the Father raised him. That is what we held.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
The ekklesia - the assembly. It was our word for the called-out gathering of people. It was not a building, and it was not an institution. Letters and a shared table tied it to every other such gathering. When a Roman governor was trying to understand what we were, the word his own law reached for was hetaeria - an illegal club, a forbidden association. That charge was never the whole of what we faced, but it shows what we looked like from outside.

The eucharistia was the thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks was given. We returned to that table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. In at least one other community, thanks was given first over the cup, then over the bread, with no story of a supper or a betrayal in the prayers - only words about the vine, about life and knowledge, and about a scattered people gathered into one. results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
We believed it because it was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. In Rome, on the day we gathered, someone read aloud from the memoirs the apostles wrote or from the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. That is how it reached us: we received it, and passed on what we received.

The people who had walked with him themselves were dying. No one could simply point anymore to someone who had been there. A letter insisted its writer stood in unbroken line with what had been handed down. A bishop insisted his office carried that same weight forward. One of our own texts says the apostles knew there would be strife over the office of oversight, and so they appointed successors.

Justin recalls that after an old man's words a flame was kindled in his soul, and he found this philosophy alone safe and profitable: “He said these things, and many others there is no time to mention now. Then he went away, telling me to think them over, and I have not seen him since. But at once a flame was kindled in my soul. A love for the prophets, and for those who are friends of Christ, took hold of me. As I turned his words over in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and useful. This is why, and this is how, I am a philosopher.”

But that is one man's account, and he had the learning to go looking. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: pahc
voice_event.text:
Polycarp of Smyrna lived it out to the end. He was an old man when the crowd called for him. They brought him before the magistrate, who pressed him to curse Christ. Polycarp answered that he had served Christ for eighty-six years, and Christ had done him no wrong - how could he blaspheme his king and savior? They burned him, then finished him with a dagger. Afterward his own church hoped to gather each year at the place where his bones were laid.

We should say this plainly: that account is his own community's memory of him. No outside witness confirms it. We also have his own letter to the Philippians, written while he was still alive. In it he tells them to be subject to the presbyters and deacons. He opens it as from Polycarp and the presbyters with him - no claim to stand alone above them. Ignatius had written to him as bishop of Smyrna. Polycarp himself does not use that title in his own letter. That is the man: he led without claiming the title, and when the moment came, he would not take back what he had spent a lifetime holding to.

voice_event.text:
We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyterion - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us. That disagreement was not a side matter. It shaped everything about how a household held together, who could lead the thanksgiving, and whether a letter from another church carried weight because one man vouched for it or because a council did.

And there is a second thing, just as important. Almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. When we tell you what we taught and how we gathered, know that you are hearing our writers, and our cities. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

glosses.plain_meaning: The overseer: the one who watches over a community's table and its unity. Whether every church should have one such man, or the elders should share that trust, was still being argued.
glosses.quick_meaning: The overseer. He watches over a community's table and its unity, where there is one. Some churches were led by a council of elders instead.
glosses.translational_sense: Modern 'bishop' names a settled office in a settled hierarchy. Here the word names a live question - some churches had such a figure, some did not, and whether every church should have one was exactly what the letters were arguing about.
false_friend: bishop as a settled office with defined powers and territory (a later picture read back)
a rung on a hierarchy ladder (the hierarchy is not yet settled)

glosses.quick_meaning: The council of elders around a bishop. It is one region's shape for leadership, not everyone's.
glosses.translational_sense: Modern 'presbytery' names a governing body or a building. Here it names one region's way of arranging leadership around a bishop, not a shape every community shared.
